claims.text: The emergence of superconductivity at low temperature is governed by the degree of local chemical short-range order.
Chemical short-range order modulates electron–phonon coupling.
Chemical short-range order modulates the electronic density of states at the Fermi level.
A moderate level of short-range order creates local lattice distortions.
Short-range-order-associated lattice distortions enhance Cooper pairing.
Moderate short-range order raises the superconducting transition temperature relative to a random atomic distribution.
Moderate short-range order may raise the superconducting critical magnetic field.
The as-cast starting state has a highly disordered, approximately random atomic arrangement.
The as-cast alloy has a primarily BCC or FCC crystal structure.
The as-cast alloy has no significant secondary intermetallic phases.
Controlled thermal annealing can increase measurable chemical short-range order in the selected alloy without causing bulk phase separation or precipitation.
Chemical short-range order reduces random-potential scattering.
Short-range-order-associated lattice distortions create locally enhanced phonon modes.
Locally enhanced phonon modes increase electron–phonon coupling strength.
Increased electron–phonon coupling raises Cooper-pairing efficiency and consequently raises Tc.
Excessive disorder causes superconducting pair breaking.
An optimal moderate degree of short-range order exists between the random and excessively ordered or disordered limits.
The annealed sample is expected to have a Tc higher than that of the as-cast sample by roughly a few kelvin.
The proposed mechanism is limited to single-phase HEAs lacking significant secondary-phase formation.
Magnetic impurities would suppress superconductivity and invalidate the proposed regime.
